title: Rereading Feels Smart. Testing Yourself Works Better.
hook_line: Rereading feels like learning. Often, it isn't.

title: Do Losses Really Hurt Twice as Much as Gains?
hook_line: Losses sting more than gains please. But how much?
full_voiceover: Losses sting more than gains please. But how much? Picture a coin flip where tails costs you a set amount. How much would heads need to pay? It's called loss aversion: a loss tends to weigh more than an equal gain. You'll often hear that losses hurt about twice as much. That number came from some early estimates, not a law of nature. Later studies found the size changes a lot with the stakes, the situation and how the choice is asked. Some researchers even argue that for small amounts, losses and gains can feel about equal. title: Does a Big Windfall Make You Happier for Good?
hook_line: Does a huge windfall make you happier for good?
full_voiceover: Does a huge windfall make you happier for good? Hedonic adaptation is the idea that after big changes, our mood tends to drift back toward its usual level. title: Why Sleeping After Studying Helps You Remember
hook_line: Study, then sleep. Your memory may thank you.

title: The Stanford Prison Experiment: Why It's Disputed
hook_line: The famous prison study? Its lesson is now disputed.
full_voiceover: The famous prison study? Its lesson is now disputed. In 1971, students were randomly assigned to be guards or prisoners in a mock prison in a university basement. The popular takeaway: give ordinary people a role and power, and they'll turn cruel on their own. Later reviews of recordings and archives suggest guards were encouraged to act tough, so the behavior wasn't purely spontaneous.
